claim: Dystroglycan (DG) requires extensive post-translational processing and O-glycosylation to function as a receptor for extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins containing laminin-G (LG) domains.
source: Dystroglycan (DG) requires extensive post-translational processing and O-glycosylation to function as a receptor for extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins containing laminin-G (LG) domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and background.

claim: Matriglycan is an elongated polysaccharide of alternating xylose (Xyl) and glucuronic acid (GlcA) that binds with high affinity to ECM proteins with LG domains.
source: Matriglycan is an elongated polysaccharide of alternating xylose (Xyl) and glucuronic acid (GlcA) that binds with high affinity to ECM proteins with LG domains and is uniquely synthesized on α-dystroglycan (α-DG) by like-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-1 (LARGE1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about matriglycan structure and function.

claim: Matriglycan is uniquely synthesized on α-dystroglycan (α-DG) by like-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-1 (LARGE1).
source: Matriglycan is an elongated polysaccharide of alternating xylose (Xyl) and glucuronic acid (GlcA) that binds with high affinity to ECM proteins with LG domains and is uniquely synthesized on α-dystroglycan (α-DG) by like-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-1 (LARGE1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about matriglycan synthesis.

claim: Defects in the post-translational processing or O-glycosylation of α-DG that result in a shorter form of matriglycan reduce the size of α-DG and decrease laminin binding, leading to various forms of muscular dystrophy.
source: Defects in the post-translational processing or O-glycosylation of α-DG that result in a shorter form of matriglycan reduce the size of α-DG and decrease laminin binding, leading to various forms of muscular dystrophy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dystroglycanopathies.

claim: Protein O-mannose kinase (POMK) is required for LARGE1 to generate full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150–250 kDa).
source: Previously, we demonstrated that protein O-mannose kinase (POMK) is required for LARGE1 to generate full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150–250 kDa) (Walimbe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: LARGE1 can only synthesize a short, non-elongated form of matriglycan in mouse skeletal muscle that lacks the DG N-terminus (α-DGN), resulting in an ~100–125 kDa α-DG.
source: Here, we show that LARGE1 can only synthesize a short, non-elongated form of matriglycan in mouse skeletal muscle that lacks the DG N-terminus (α-DGN), resulting in an ~100–125 kDa α-DG.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The ~100–125 kDa α-DG form binds laminin and maintains specific force.
source: This smaller form of α-DG binds laminin and maintains specific force but does not prevent muscle pathophysiology, including reduced force production after eccentric contractions (ECs) or abnormalities in the neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript showing laminin overlay and force measurements.

claim: The ~100–125 kDa α-DG form does not prevent muscle pathophysiology, including reduced force production after eccentric contractions (ECs).
source: This smaller form of α-DG binds laminin and maintains specific force but does not prevent muscle pathophysiology, including reduced force production after eccentric contractions (ECs) or abnormalities in the neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing force deficits after eccentric contractions.

claim: The ~100–125 kDa α-DG form does not prevent abnormalities in the neuromuscular junctions.
source: This smaller form of α-DG binds laminin and maintains specific force but does not prevent muscle pathophysiology, including reduced force production after eccentric contractions (ECs) or abnormalities in the neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NMJ abnormalities in M-α-DGN KO mice.

claim: α-DGN is required for LARGE1 to extend matriglycan to its full mature length on α-DG and thus prevent muscle pathophysiology.
source: Collectively, our study demonstrates that α-DGN, like POMK, is required for LARGE1 to extend matriglycan to its full mature length on α-DG and thus prevent muscle pathophysiology.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: The basement membrane is a specialized network of extracellular matrix (ECM) macromolecules that surrounds epithelium, endothelium, muscle, fat, and neurons.
source: The basement membrane is a specialized network of extracellular matrix (ECM) macromolecules that surrounds epithelium, endothelium, muscle, fat, and neurons (Rowe and Weiss, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Skeletal muscle cells are bound to the basement membrane through transmembrane receptors, including dystroglycan (DG) and integrins.
source: Skeletal muscle cells are bound to the basement membrane through transmembrane receptors, including dystroglycan (DG) and integrins, which help maintain the structural and functional integrity of the muscle cell membrane (Ibraghimov-Beskrovnaya et al., 1992; Han et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DG is a central component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC).
source: DG is a central component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: DG is encoded by a single gene, DAG1, and cleaved into α- and β-subunits (α-DG and β-DG, respectively) by post-translational processing.
source: It is encoded by a single gene, DAG1, and cleaved into α- and β-subunits (α-DG and β-DG, respectively) by post-translational processing (Ibraghimov-Beskrovnaya et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Extensive O-glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG) is required for normal muscle function.
source: Extensive O-glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG) is required for normal muscle function, and defects in this process result in various forms of muscular dystrophy (Michele et al., 2002; Ohtsubo and Marth, 2006; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Praissman et al., 2016; Sheikh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Defects in O-glycosylation of α-DG result in various forms of muscular dystrophy.
source: Extensive O-glycosylation of α-dystroglycan (α-DG) is required for normal muscle function, and defects in this process result in various forms of muscular dystrophy (Michele et al., 2002; Ohtsubo and Marth, 2006; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Praissman et al., 2016; Sheikh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: α-DG binds to ECM ligands containing laminin-G (LG) domains (e.g., laminin, agrin, perlecan) which are essential components of the basement membrane.
source: α-DG binds to ECM ligands containing laminin-G (LG) domains (e.g., laminin, agrin, perlecan) which are essential components of the basement membrane (Michele et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DG physically links the cell membrane to the basement membrane.
source: DG, thereby, physically links the cell membrane to the basement membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DG function.

claim: The physical linkage between cell membrane and basement membrane requires the synthesis of matriglycan, a heteropolysaccharide [-GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-]n, on α-DG by the bifunctional glycosyltransferase, like-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-1 (LARGE1).
source: This process requires the synthesis of matriglycan, a heteropolysaccharide [-GlcA-β1,3-Xyl-α1,3-]n, on α-DG by the bifunctional glycosyltransferase, like-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-1 (LARGE1) (Inamori et al., 2012; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Ohtsubo and Marth, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: A single glucuronic acid-xylose disaccharide (GlcA-Xyl) repeat binds with high-affinity to laminin-α2 LG4,5.
source: Structural studies have shown that a single glucuronic acid-xylose disaccharide (GlcA-Xyl) repeat binds with high-affinity to laminin-α2 LG4,5, and there is a direct correlation between the number of GlcA-Xyl repeats on α-DG and its binding capacity for ECM ligands (Briggs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: There is a direct correlation between the number of GlcA-Xyl repeats on α-DG and its binding capacity for ECM ligands.
source: Structural studies have shown that a single glucuronic acid-xylose disaccharide (GlcA-Xyl) repeat binds with high-affinity to laminin-α2 LG4,5, and there is a direct correlation between the number of GlcA-Xyl repeats on α-DG and its binding capacity for ECM ligands (Briggs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claim: During skeletal muscle differentiation, LARGE1 elongates matriglycan, thereby increasing the binding capacity of matriglycan for ECM ligands.
source: During skeletal muscle differentiation, LARGE1 elongates matriglycan, thereby increasing the binding capacity of matriglycan for ECM ligands and allowing matriglycan to serve as a matrix scaffold that is required for skeletal muscle function (Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Matriglycan serves as a matrix scaffold that is required for skeletal muscle function.
source: During skeletal muscle differentiation, LARGE1 elongates matriglycan, thereby increasing the binding capacity of matriglycan for ECM ligands and allowing matriglycan to serve as a matrix scaffold that is required for skeletal muscle function (Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Matriglycan synthesis requires the addition of core M3 trisaccharide (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) onto specific threonine residues on α-DG in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Matriglycan synthesis requires the addition of core M3 trisaccharide (GalNAc-β1,3-GlcNAc-β1,4-Man) onto specific threonine residues on α-DG in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Sheikh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Once core M3 is synthesized, the glycosylation-specific kinase, protein O-mannose kinase (POMK) phosphorylates mannose of core M3.
source: Once core M3 is synthesized, the glycosylation-specific kinase, protein O-mannose kinase (POMK) phosphorylates mannose of core M3, and this is required for the subsequent addition of full-length, high-molecular weight forms of matriglycan onto the O-mannose linked modification (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Jae et al., 2013; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Phosphorylation of mannose of core M3 by POMK is required for the subsequent addition of full-length, high-molecular weight forms of matriglycan onto the O-mannose linked modification.
source: Once core M3 is synthesized, the glycosylation-specific kinase, protein O-mannose kinase (POMK) phosphorylates mannose of core M3, and this is required for the subsequent addition of full-length, high-molecular weight forms of matriglycan onto the O-mannose linked modification (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015; Hohenester, 2019; Jae et al., 2013; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the absence of core M3 phosphorylation by POMK, LARGE1 synthesizes a short, non-elongated form of matriglycan on α-DG.
source: In the absence of core M3 phosphorylation by POMK, LARGE1 synthesizes a short, non-elongated form of matriglycan on α-DG (Walimbe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A loss of function in the post-translational addition of matriglycan leads to a group of disorders known as dystroglycanopathies, congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies with or without brain and eye abnormalities.
source: Notably, a loss of function in the post-translational addition of matriglycan leads to a group of disorders known as dystroglycanopathies, congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies with or without brain and eye abnormalities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dystroglycanopathies.

claim: Disease severity in dystroglycanopathies is dependent on the ability of matriglycan to bind ECM ligands, which is dictated by its length and expression.
source: Disease severity is dependent on the ability of matriglycan to bind ECM ligands, which is dictated by its length and expression (Goddeeris et al., 2013): matriglycan that is of low molecular weight (e.g., short) can cause muscular dystrophy, even if its capacity to bind LG domains is not completely lost (Puckett et al., 2009; Hara et al., 2011a; Hara et al., 2011b; Carss et al., 2013; Cirak et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2015; Walimbe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Matriglycan that is of low molecular weight (e.g., short) can cause muscular dystrophy, even if its capacity to bind LG domains is not completely lost.
source: Disease severity is dependent on the ability of matriglycan to bind ECM ligands, which is dictated by its length and expression (Goddeeris et al., 2013): matriglycan that is of low molecular weight (e.g., short) can cause muscular dystrophy, even if its capacity to bind LG domains is not completely lost (Puckett et al., 2009; Hara et al., 2011a; Hara et al., 2011b; Carss et al., 2013; Cirak et al., 2013; Dong et al., 2015; Walimbe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: α-DG is composed of three distinct domains: the N-terminal (α-DGN) domain, a central mucin-like domain, and the C-terminal domain.
source: α-DG is composed of three distinct domains: the N-terminal (α-DGN) domain, a central mucin-like domain, and the C-terminal domain (Figure 1; Ibraghimov-Beskrovnaya et al., 1992; Brancaccio et al., 1995; Brancaccio et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: α-DGN serves as a binding site for LARGE1 in the Golgi.
source: α-DGN serves as a binding site for LARGE1 in the Golgi and is required for the subsequent functional glycosylation of the mucin-like domain of α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: α-DGN is required for the subsequent functional glycosylation of the mucin-like domain of α-DG.
source: α-DGN serves as a binding site for LARGE1 in the Golgi and is required for the subsequent functional glycosylation of the mucin-like domain of α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice were slightly lower in weight than WT littermate (control) mice at 12 weeks of age.
source: M-α-DGN KO mice were slightly lower in weight than WT littermate (control) mice at 12 weeks of age, and they exhibited decreased forelimb grip strength as well (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice exhibited decreased forelimb grip strength at 12 weeks of age.
source: M-α-DGN KO mice were slightly lower in weight than WT littermate (control) mice at 12 weeks of age, and they exhibited decreased forelimb grip strength as well (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice showed characteristic features of muscular dystrophy, including an increase in centrally nucleated fibers.
source: M-α-DGN KO mice showed characteristic features of muscular dystrophy, including an increase in centrally nucleated fibers (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence analyses of M-α-DGN KO muscle showed reduced levels of matriglycan relative to controls.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of M-α-DGN KO muscle showed reduced levels of matriglycan relative to controls, but a similar expression of β-DG, the transmembrane subunit of DG (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: M-α-DGN KO muscle showed similar expression of β-DG compared to controls.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of M-α-DGN KO muscle showed reduced levels of matriglycan relative to controls, but a similar expression of β-DG, the transmembrane subunit of DG (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice expresses a shorter form of matriglycan which results in an ~100–125 kDa α-DG.
source: Immunoblot analysis demonstrated that skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice expresses a shorter form of matriglycan which results in an ~100–125 kDa α-DG, a decrease in the molecular weight of the core α-DG, and no change in β-DG (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice show a decrease in the molecular weight of the core α-DG.
source: Immunoblot analysis demonstrated that skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice expresses a shorter form of matriglycan which results in an ~100–125 kDa α-DG, a decrease in the molecular weight of the core α-DG, and no change in β-DG (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice show no change in β-DG molecular weight.
source: Immunoblot analysis demonstrated that skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice expresses a shorter form of matriglycan which results in an ~100–125 kDa α-DG, a decrease in the molecular weight of the core α-DG, and no change in β-DG (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No matriglycan is seen in Largemyd mice which have a deletion in Large1.
source: No matriglycan is seen in Largemyd mice which have a deletion in Large1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Skeletal muscle from control mice showed a broad band centered at ~100–250 kDa in laminin overlay, indicative of α-DG-laminin binding.
source: Skeletal muscle from control mice showed a broad band centered at ~100–250 kDa, indicative of α-DG-laminin binding; in contrast, we observed laminin binding at ~100–125 kDa in M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Laminin binding was observed at ~100–125 kDa in M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle.
source: Skeletal muscle from control mice showed a broad band centered at ~100–250 kDa, indicative of α-DG-laminin binding; in contrast, we observed laminin binding at ~100–125 kDa in M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ~100–125 kDa band in M-α-DGN KO muscle is matriglycan-positive α-DG.
source: To further confirm that the ~100–125 kDa band seen with anti-matriglycan antibodies in M-α-DGN KO muscle is matriglycan-positive α-DG, we digested it overnight with β-glucuronidase (Thermotoga maritima) and α-xylosidase (Sulfolobus solfataricus). Immunoblot analysis with anti-matriglycan antibodies and laminin overlay revealed that ~100–125 kDa was completely lost after enzymatic digestion, indicating that the ~100–125 kDa band is indeed matriglycan-positive α-DG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic digestion experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ~100–125 kDa α-DG was completely lost after enzymatic digestion with β-glucuronidase and α-xylosidase.
source: Immunoblot analysis with anti-matriglycan antibodies and laminin overlay revealed that ~100–125 kDa was completely lost after enzymatic digestion, indicating that the ~100–125 kDa band is indeed matriglycan-positive α-DG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by enzymatic digestion data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sensitivity of ~100–125 kDa α-DG to enzymatic digestion demonstrates that matriglycan is not capped like brain α-DG.
source: The sensitivity of ~100–125 kDa α-DG to enzymatic digestion also demonstrates that matriglycan is not capped like brain α-DG (Sheikh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enzymatic digestion data and comparison to brain α-DG.

claim: NMJs in adult control mice demonstrate a normal pretzel-like morphology.
source: The NMJs in adult control mice demonstrate a normal pretzel-like morphology whereas NMJs from M-α-DGN KO mice display a variety of abnormalities, including a granular appearance and AChR-rich streaks extending beyond the pre-synaptic terminal (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by NMJ morphology data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NMJs from M-α-DGN KO mice display a variety of abnormalities, including a granular appearance and AChR-rich streaks extending beyond the pre-synaptic terminal.
source: The NMJs in adult control mice demonstrate a normal pretzel-like morphology whereas NMJs from M-α-DGN KO mice display a variety of abnormalities, including a granular appearance and AChR-rich streaks extending beyond the pre-synaptic terminal (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by NMJ morphology data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Post-synaptic morphology in adult M-α-DGN KO mice was predominately irregular in the tibialis anterior (TA), extensor digitorum longus (EDL), and soleus (SOL) muscles.
source: Post-synaptic morphology in adult M-α-DGN KO mice was predominately irregular in the tibialis anterior (TA), extensor digitorum longus (EDL), and soleus (SOL) muscles (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by NMJ morphology scoring data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The overall synaptic size did not differ between controls and M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: Although the overall synaptic size did not differ between controls and M-α-DGN KO mice, the dispersion of AChR clusters was greater in the M-α-DGN KOs (Figure 3B), in line with an increased percentage of plaque-like formations and AChR extensions that projected beyond the nerve terminal.
evidence: This is supported by NMJ morphology data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The dispersion of AChR clusters was greater in M-α-DGN KO mice compared to controls.
source: Although the overall synaptic size did not differ between controls and M-α-DGN KO mice, the dispersion of AChR clusters was greater in the M-α-DGN KOs (Figure 3B), in line with an increased percentage of plaque-like formations and AChR extensions that projected beyond the nerve terminal.
evidence: This is supported by NMJ morphology data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All NMJs from M-α-DGN KO mice were fully innervated.
source: Despite the post-synaptic abnormalities, all NMJs from M-α-DGN KO mice were fully innervated.
evidence: This is supported by NMJ analysis data.

claim: Muscle mass was comparable between control and M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: Muscle mass and CSA were comparable between control and M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by muscle mass data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) was comparable between control and M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: Muscle mass and CSA were comparable between control and M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by CSA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The production of absolute isometric tetanic force was significantly lower in M-α-DGN KO mice compared to control mice.
source: Although the production of absolute isometric tetanic force was significantly lower in M-α-DGN KO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4C), specific forces were comparable between the two groups when normalized to muscle CSA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by force production data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Specific forces were comparable between control and M-α-DGN KO mice when normalized to muscle CSA.
source: Although the production of absolute isometric tetanic force was significantly lower in M-α-DGN KO mice compared to control mice (Figure 4C), specific forces were comparable between the two groups when normalized to muscle CSA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by specific force data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lengthening contraction-induced force reduction in M-α-DGN KO EDL remained greater than those from control EDL for the entire 60 min that muscles were assessed.
source: Lengthening contraction-induced force reduction in M-α-DGN KO EDL remained greater than those from control EDL for the entire 60 min that muscles were assessed (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The short form of matriglycan in M-α-DGN KO EDL enables force production but cannot prevent force reduction caused by lengthening contractions.
source: These results suggest that the short form of matriglycan on α-DG in M-α-DGN KO EDL enables force production but cannot prevent force reduction caused by lengthening contractions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the force production and eccentric contraction data.

claim: POMK KO skeletal muscle expresses a short form of matriglycan, similar to M-α-DGN KO muscle.
source: POMK KO skeletal muscle also expresses a short form of matriglycan, similar to M-α-DGN KO muscle.
evidence: This is based on comparison to previous work on POMK KO mice.

claim: The short form of matriglycan in POMK KO skeletal muscle maintains force production but cannot prevent lengthening contraction-induced force decline.
source: The short form of matriglycan in POMK KO skeletal muscle maintains force production but similarly cannot prevent lengthening contraction-induced force decline (Walimbe et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There were no significant differences in lengthening contraction-induced force deficits between M-α-DGN KO and POMK KO mice.
source: We did not observe significant differences in lengthening contraction-induced force deficits between the two mouse strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparative force deficit data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Muscle with similar size matriglycan exhibits similar force production and lengthening contraction-induced force decline.
source: These results suggest that muscle with similar size matriglycan exhibits similar force production and lengthening contraction-induced force decline.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between M-α-DGN KO and POMK KO mice.

claim: Constitutive deletion of DG in mice causes embryonic lethality due to disruption of Reichert's membrane.
source: Constitutive deletion of DG in mice causes embryonic lethality due to disruption of Reichert's membrane, an extraembryonic basement membrane required for in utero development (Williamson et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Deletion of α-DGN in mice causes embryonic lethality.
source: Deletion of α-DGN in mice also causes embryonic lethality (de Greef et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mice that are heterozygous for α-DGN deletion (Dag1wt/Δα-DGN) are viable.
source: However, mice that are heterozygous for α-DGN deletion (Dag1wt/Δα-DGN) are viable and express α-DG of two different sizes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) corresponding to both wild-type (WT) and the α-DGN-deleted (Δα-DGN) forms of DG.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Heterozygous α-DGN deletion mice express α-DG of two different sizes corresponding to both wild-type (WT) and the α-DGN-deleted (Δα-DGN) forms of DG.
source: However, mice that are heterozygous for α-DGN deletion (Dag1wt/Δα-DGN) are viable and express α-DG of two different sizes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) corresponding to both wild-type (WT) and the α-DGN-deleted (Δα-DGN) forms of DG.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of quadriceps muscles from M-Dag1 KO mice showed the absence of β-DG-positive fibers.
source: To assess the presence of DG, we performed immunostaining of quadriceps muscles from 12-week-old M-Dag1 KO mice, which showed the absence of β-DG-positive fibers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: α-DG derived from skeletal muscle was absent in M-Dag1 KO mice.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that α-DG derived from skeletal muscle was absent in M-Dag1 KO mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Peripheral nerve-derived α-DG of 110 kDa is observed in M-Dag1 KO mice in the presence of EDTA.
source: However, consistent with prior reports, peripheral nerve-derived α-DG of 110 kDa is observed in M-Dag1 KO mice in the presence of EDTA, which improves the extraction of matriglycan-positive α-DG (Saito et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data and citation to previous work.

claim: Muscle-specific force was significantly decreased in M-Dag1 KO mice.
source: To assess muscle function, we evaluated muscle-specific force and lengthening contraction-induced reduction in force ex vivo, which showed that muscle-specific force was significantly decreased and that muscles were more susceptible to lengthening contraction-induced force decline in the absence of DG (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by force measurement data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: M-Dag1 KO muscles were more susceptible to lengthening contraction-induced force decline.
source: To assess muscle function, we evaluated muscle-specific force and lengthening contraction-induced reduction in force ex vivo, which showed that muscle-specific force was significantly decreased and that muscles were more susceptible to lengthening contraction-induced force decline in the absence of DG (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: M-Dag1 KO mice harbor a more complete loss of DG in muscle than the previously generated MCKCre; Dag1flox/flox mouse model.
source: Collectively, these results show that M-Dag1 KO mice harbor a more complete loss of DG in muscle than the previously generated mouse model that deleted DG with cre driven by the muscle creatine kinase (MCK) promotor (MCKCre; Dag1flox/flox) harboring muscle-specific deletion of DG (Cohn et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to previous mouse models and supported by citation.

claim: Matriglycan of similar size was produced in M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK DG-E as in M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: However, we found that matriglycan of similar size was produced in M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK DG-E as in M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis of quadriceps muscles from M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK DG-E showed decreased immunoreactivity to matriglycan-positive muscle fibers but restored expression of β-DG.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of quadriceps muscles from M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK DG-E showed decreased immunoreactivity to matriglycan-positive muscle fibers but restored expression of β-DG (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immunoblot analysis of skeletal muscle from M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK-DG-E showed expression of α-DG containing matriglycan around ~100–125 kDa.
source: Immunoblot analysis of skeletal muscle from M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK-DG-E showed expression of α-DG containing matriglycan around ~100–125 kDa (Figure 5C), which was the same size as α-DG with the short form of matriglycan in M-α-DGN KO muscle (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The molecular weight of α-DG was decreased in muscle from M-Dag1 KO mice injected with AAV-MCK-DG-E, similar to that observed in M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: The molecular weight of α-DG was decreased in muscle from M-Dag1 KO mice, similar to that observed in M-α-DGN KO mice, whereas the molecular weight of β-DG was unchanged relative to M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5C and comparison to Figure 2C.

claim: Laminin binding was observed at ~100–125 kDa in muscle from M-Dag1 KO + AAV MCK DG-E mice.
source: We also observed laminin binding at ~100–125 kDa in muscle from M-Dag1 KO + AAV MCK DG-E mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The specific force was comparable in M-Dag1 KO + AAV MCK DG-E and M-Dag1 KO mice.
source: We observed that the specific force was comparable in M-Dag1 KO + AAV MCK DG-E and M-Dag1 KO mice (Figure 5D) and that the two groups exhibited similar amounts of lengthening contraction-induced force decline (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by force measurement data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: M-Dag1 KO + AAV MCK DG-E and M-Dag1 KO mice exhibited similar amounts of lengthening contraction-induced force decline.
source: We observed that the specific force was comparable in M-Dag1 KO + AAV MCK DG-E and M-Dag1 KO mice (Figure 5D) and that the two groups exhibited similar amounts of lengthening contraction-induced force decline (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: AAV-mediated delivery of exogenous DG lacking the α-DGN into M-Dag1 KO mice produces a short-form matriglycan.
source: Therefore, these data demonstrate that AAV-mediated delivery of exogenous DG lacking the α-DGN into M-Dag1 KO mice also produces a short-form matriglycan and such mice exhibit similar muscle function as M-α-DGN KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from AAV injection experiments.

claim: Mice with AAV-mediated delivery of exogenous DG lacking the α-DGN exhibit similar muscle function as M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: Therefore, these data demonstrate that AAV-mediated delivery of exogenous DG lacking the α-DGN into M-Dag1 KO mice also produces a short-form matriglycan and such mice exhibit similar muscle function as M-α-DGN KO mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from AAV injection experiments.

claim: DG lacking the α-DGN expresses a short form of matriglycan.
source: Our studies show that DG lacking the α-DGN expresses a short form of matriglycan; this suggests that α-DGN is necessary to produce full-length matriglycan.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from multiple experiments.

claim: α-DGN is necessary to produce full-length matriglycan.
source: Our studies show that DG lacking the α-DGN expresses a short form of matriglycan; this suggests that α-DGN is necessary to produce full-length matriglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: H&E staining in M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-CMV α-DGN was unchanged from M-α-DGN KO mice.
source: H&E staining in M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-CMV α-DGN was unchanged from M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 2B and Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Quadriceps muscles from M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-CMV α-DGN showed a reduced intensity of matriglycan relative to littermate controls.
source: Quadriceps muscles from M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-CMV α-DGN showed a reduced intensity of matriglycan relative to littermate controls (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Immunoblot analysis of M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-CMV α-DGN showed that α-DG had a molecular weight of ~100–125 kDa.
source: Immunoblot analysis of these mice showed that α-DG had a molecular weight of ~100–125 kDa, whereas β-DG remained unchanged (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Laminin binding was observed at ~100–125 kDa in M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle infected with AAV-CMV α-DGN.
source: Laminin binding was observed at ~100–125 kDa in M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle infected with AAV-CMV α-DGN (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expressing α-DGN in M-α-DGN KO mice did not alter specific force.
source: Expressing α-DGN in M-α-DGN KO mice did not alter specific force or improve force deficits induced by lengthening contractions (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by force measurement data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expressing α-DGN in M-α-DGN KO mice did not improve force deficits induced by lengthening contractions.
source: Expressing α-DGN in M-α-DGN KO mice did not alter specific force or improve force deficits induced by lengthening contractions (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Supplementing M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle with α-DGN fails to produce full-length matriglycan.
source: Thus, supplementing M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle with α-DGN fails to produce full-length matriglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from AAV-CMV α-DGN injection experiments.

claim: Immunoblot analysis of skeletal muscle from control mice and those overexpressing free α-DGN (α-DGN transgenic [α-DGN Tg]) showed that α-DG had a reduced molecular weight of ~100–125 kDa.
source: To test if excessive free α-DGN interferes with the binding of endogenous α-DGN to LARGE1, we analyzed immunoblots of skeletal muscle from control mice and those overexpressing free α-DGN (α-DGN transgenic [α-DGN Tg]). Immunoblot analysis of these mice showed that α-DG had a reduced molecular weight of ~100–125 kDa, whereas β-DG remained unchanged (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Free α-DGN interferes with the elongation of matriglycan.
source: This biochemical phenotype is similar to that observed in the skeletal muscles of M-α-DGN KO mice and demonstrates that free α-DGN interferes with the elongation of matriglycan, but that LARGE1 can still synthesize a short form of matriglycan on α-DG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the α-DGN Tg mouse data.

claim: LARGE1 can still synthesize a short form of matriglycan on α-DG even when free α-DGN interferes with elongation.
source: This biochemical phenotype is similar to that observed in the skeletal muscles of M-α-DGN KO mice and demonstrates that free α-DGN interferes with the elongation of matriglycan, but that LARGE1 can still synthesize a short form of matriglycan on α-DG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the α-DGN Tg mouse data.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-MCK-Large1 demonstrated no change in the molecular weight of α-DG and β-DG relative to M-α-DGN KO.
source: M-α-DGN KO mice injected with AAV-MCK-Large1 demonstrated no change in the molecular weight of α-DG and β-DG relative to M-α-DGN KO. A laminin overlay using laminin-111 also showed no change (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even if LARGE1 is overexpressed, full-length matriglycan cannot be produced without α-DGN.
source: These results indicate that even if LARGE1 is overexpressed, full-length matriglycan cannot be produced without α-DGN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the AAV-MCK-Large1 injection data.

claim: The ability of matriglycan to bind ECM ligands correlates with its length.
source: The ability of matriglycan to bind ECM ligands correlates with its length (Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: M-α-DGN KO mice showed a significantly higher percent deficit (70.2%±5.7) at the eighth EC compared to C57 (41.7%±8.0) and Dag1T190M (41.6%±6.7) mice.
source: M-α-DGN KO mice showed a significantly higher percent deficit (70.2%±5.7) compared to C57 (41.7%±8.0) and Dag1T190M (41.6%±6.7) mice, with no difference observed between the latter groups.
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There was no difference in percent deficit at the eighth EC between C57 and Dag1T190M mice.
source: M-α-DGN KO mice showed a significantly higher percent deficit (70.2%±5.7) compared to C57 (41.7%±8.0) and Dag1T190M (41.6%±6.7) mice, with no difference observed between the latter groups.
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Laminin overlay assay in skeletal muscle showed α-DG laminin binding at ~150–250 kDa in skeletal muscle from C57 mice.
source: Laminin overlay assay in skeletal muscle showed α-DG laminin binding at ~150–250 kDa in skeletal muscle from C57 mice, ~100–150 kDa in skeletal muscle from Dag1T190M mice, and ~100–125 kDa in skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Laminin overlay assay showed α-DG laminin binding at ~100–150 kDa in skeletal muscle from Dag1T190M mice.
source: Laminin overlay assay in skeletal muscle showed α-DG laminin binding at ~150–250 kDa in skeletal muscle from C57 mice, ~100–150 kDa in skeletal muscle from Dag1T190M mice, and ~100–125 kDa in skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by laminin overlay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The percentage of centrally nucleated fibers differed significantly in Dag1T190M (1.73%±0.31) and M-α-DGN KO (9.28%±2.41) mice compared to C57 mice (1.22%±0.15).
source: Moreover, the percentage of centrally nucleated fibers differed significantly in Dag1T190M (1.73%±0.31) and M-α-DGN KO (9.28%±2.41) mice compared to C57 mice (1.22%±0.15) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The reduction of laminin-binding activity of α-DG is thought to be the main cause of dystroglycanopathy.
source: The reduction of laminin-binding activity of α-DG is thought to be the main cause of dystroglycanopathy (Kanagawa et al., 2009; Goddeeris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A reduced binding capacity (relative Bmax) for laminin-111 was observed in solid-phase binding analyses in skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO and Dag1T190M mice compared to skeletal muscle from C57 mice (10.7-fold and 2.3-fold difference relative to WT, respectively).
source: Indeed, we observed a reduced binding capacity (relative Bmax) for laminin-111 in solid-phase binding analyses in skeletal muscle from M-α-DGN KO and Dag1T190M mice compared to skeletal muscle from C57 mice (10.7-fold and 2.3-fold difference relative to WT, respectively) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by solid-phase binding assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The binding capacity of skeletal muscle from Dag1T190M and M-α-DGN KO mice was higher than that of Large1myd muscle.
source: However, the binding capacity of skeletal muscle from Dag1T190M and M-α-DGN KO mice was higher than that of Large1myd muscle (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by solid-phase binding assay data shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: M-α-DGN KO and Dag1T190M displayed a greater dissociation constant compared to controls.
source: M-α-DGN KO and Dag1T190M also displayed a greater dissociation constant (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by solid-phase binding assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Matriglycan-positive α-DG of at least ~150 kDa is sufficient to prevent force decline from lengthening contractions and significant dystrophic changes, despite a 45% reduction in laminin-binding activity.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that matriglycan-positive α-DG of at least ~150 kDa is sufficient to prevent force decline from lengthening contractions and significant dystrophic changes, despite a 45% reduction in laminin-binding activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data from different mouse models.

claim: LARGE1 synthesizes a non-elongated form of matriglycan on α-DG lacking α-DGN (i.e., α-DGN-deleted DG).
source: We now show that LARGE1 synthesizes a non-elongated form of matriglycan on α-DG lacking α-DGN (i.e., α-DGN-deleted DG).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The short form of matriglycan on α-DG lacking α-DGN binds laminin and maintains specific force.
source: This short form of matriglycan binds laminin and maintains specific force.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from force measurements and laminin overlay assays.

claim: The short form of matriglycan on α-DG lacking α-DGN fails to prevent reduced force production after ECs.
source: However, it fails to prevent reduced force production after ECs, NMJ abnormalities, or dystrophic changes in muscle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from eccentric contraction experiments.

claim: The short form of matriglycan on α-DG lacking α-DGN fails to prevent NMJ abnormalities.
source: However, it fails to prevent reduced force production after ECs, NMJ abnormalities, or dystrophic changes in muscle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from NMJ morphology analysis.

claim: The short form of matriglycan on α-DG lacking α-DGN fails to prevent dystrophic changes in muscle.
source: However, it fails to prevent reduced force production after ECs, NMJ abnormalities, or dystrophic changes in muscle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from histological analysis.

claim: LARGE1 requires α-DGN to generate full-length matriglycan in skeletal muscle.
source: Collectively, our study shows that LARGE1 requires α-DGN to generate full-length matriglycan in skeletal muscle, but the synthesis of a shorter form of matriglycan can proceed independently of this domain.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: The synthesis of a shorter form of matriglycan can proceed independently of α-DGN.
source: Collectively, our study shows that LARGE1 requires α-DGN to generate full-length matriglycan in skeletal muscle, but the synthesis of a shorter form of matriglycan can proceed independently of this domain.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: The interaction between LARGE1 and α-DGN holds the enzyme-substrate complex together over multiple cycles of sugar addition.
source: Our results suggest that the interaction between LARGE1 and α-DGN holds the enzyme-substrate complex together over multiple cycles of sugar addition.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The generation of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150–250 kDa) by LARGE1 requires both POMK and α-DGN.
source: Thus, the generation of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150–250 kDa) by LARGE1 requires both POMK and α-DGN; in the absence of either, LARGE1 synthesizes a shorter form of matriglycan.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study and previous work on POMK.

claim: In the absence of either POMK or α-DGN, LARGE1 synthesizes a shorter form of matriglycan.
source: Thus, the generation of full-length matriglycan on α-DG (~150–250 kDa) by LARGE1 requires both POMK and α-DGN; in the absence of either, LARGE1 synthesizes a shorter form of matriglycan.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study and previous work on POMK.

claim: The interaction between LARGE1 and α-DGN is essential for efficient matriglycan polymerization.
source: Thus, the interaction between LARGE1 and α-DGN is essential for efficient matriglycan polymerization.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Muscle-specific deletion of α-DGN resulted in the production of short forms of matriglycan on α-DG (~100–125 kDa).
source: In our study, muscle-specific deletion of α-DGN resulted in the production of short forms of matriglycan on α-DG (~100–125 kDa).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Mice lacking α-DGN exhibited low body weight and grip strength.
source: Mice lacking α-DGN exhibited low body weight and grip strength, and histological characterization of quadriceps muscles revealed mild muscular dystrophy and a lack of homogeneous matriglycan expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from body weight and grip strength measurements.

claim: Histological characterization of quadriceps muscles from mice lacking α-DGN revealed mild muscular dystrophy and a lack of homogeneous matriglycan expression.
source: Mice lacking α-DGN exhibited low body weight and grip strength, and histological characterization of quadriceps muscles revealed mild muscular dystrophy and a lack of homogeneous matriglycan expression.
evidence: This is supported by histological and immunofluorescence data.

claim: M-α-DGN KO muscle was susceptible to lengthening contraction-induced force decline, although specific force was maintained.
source: Physiological examination revealed that M-α-DGN KO muscle was susceptible to lengthening contraction-induced force decline, although specific force was maintained.
evidence: This is supported by force measurement data.

claim: α-DG lacking α-DGN produces short forms of matriglycan, which do not prevent dystrophic muscle changes in this mouse model.
source: These results are consistent with those obtained when α-DGN-deleted DG was expressed in muscle-specific DG null mice and confirm that α-DG lacking α-DGN produces short forms of matriglycan, which do not prevent dystrophic muscle changes in this mouse model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: DG in the post-synaptic membrane is known to play a key role in synaptic maturation.
source: Furthermore, DG in the post-synaptic membrane is known to play a key role in synaptic maturation (Nishimune et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The NMJs in M-α-DGN KO mice were abnormal and irregularly shaped.
source: However, the NMJs in M-α-DGN KO mice in our study were abnormal and irregularly shaped.
evidence: This is supported by NMJ morphology data.

claim: Both DG and full-length matriglycan are required for synaptic maturation.
source: This indicates both that DG and full-length matriglycan are required for synaptic maturation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NMJ abnormalities observed in M-α-DGN KO mice.

claim: Rescuing M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle with α-DGN failed to restore the expression of full-length matriglycan.
source: If LARGE1 binding to α-DGN enables its ability to elongate matriglycan, then we would expect that rescuing M-α-DGN KO skeletal muscle with α-DGN would restore the expression of full-length matriglycan. However, this failed to occur and suggests that restoring α-DGN expression alone is not sufficient for LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AAV-CMV α-DGN injection experiments.

claim: Restoring α-DGN expression alone is not sufficient for LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan.
source: However, this failed to occur and suggests that restoring α-DGN expression alone is not sufficient for LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from AAV-CMV α-DGN injection experiments.

claim: The ability of LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan requires α-DG with α-DGN.
source: These results indicate that the ability of LARGE1 to elongate matriglycan requires α-DG with α-DGN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Matriglycan is not elongated when α-DGN is deleted, even when LARGE1 is overexpressed.
source: This finding is consistent with data showing that matriglycan is not elongated when α-DGN is deleted, even when LARGE1 is overexpressed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from AAV-MCK-Large1 injection experiments.

claim: α-DGN acts as a recognition site for the glycosyltransferase LARGE1.
source: Therefore, α-DGN acts as a recognition site for the glycosyltransferase LARGE1 and establishes a model where α-DGN, together with phosphorylated core M3, anchors LARGE1 to the matriglycan production site to enable its synthesis and elongation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the experimental findings.

claim: α-DGN, together with phosphorylated core M3, anchors LARGE1 to the matriglycan production site to enable its synthesis and elongation.
source: Therefore, α-DGN acts as a recognition site for the glycosyltransferase LARGE1 and establishes a model where α-DGN, together with phosphorylated core M3, anchors LARGE1 to the matriglycan production site to enable its synthesis and elongation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The molecular recognition of α-DGN by LARGE1 is considered essential for the expression of functional α-DG.
source: Notably, although the molecular recognition of α-DGN by LARGE1 is considered essential for the expression of functional α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004), our results show that LARGE1 can synthesize a short non-elongated form of matriglycan in the absence of α-DGN, indicating that LARGE1 does not need to interact with α-DGN to function.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LARGE1 can synthesize a short non-elongated form of matriglycan in the absence of α-DGN.
source: Notably, although the molecular recognition of α-DGN by LARGE1 is considered essential for the expression of functional α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004), our results show that LARGE1 can synthesize a short non-elongated form of matriglycan in the absence of α-DGN, indicating that LARGE1 does not need to interact with α-DGN to function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: LARGE1 does not need to interact with α-DGN to function.
source: Notably, although the molecular recognition of α-DGN by LARGE1 is considered essential for the expression of functional α-DG (Kanagawa et al., 2004), our results show that LARGE1 can synthesize a short non-elongated form of matriglycan in the absence of α-DGN, indicating that LARGE1 does not need to interact with α-DGN to function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice showed an increased force deficit compared to muscle from C57 mice.
source: Muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice showed an increased force deficit and a 7.6-fold increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice, indicating that the short form of matriglycan does not prevent dystrophic changes.
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data.

claim: Muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice showed a 7.6-fold increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice.
source: Muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice showed an increased force deficit and a 7.6-fold increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice, indicating that the short form of matriglycan does not prevent dystrophic changes.
evidence: This is supported by histological data.

claim: The short form of matriglycan does not prevent dystrophic changes.
source: Muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice showed an increased force deficit and a 7.6-fold increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice, indicating that the short form of matriglycan does not prevent dystrophic changes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Despite the lower amount of matriglycan in muscle from Dag1T190M mice compared to that from C57 mice, the force deficit was not different between the two groups.
source: However, despite the lower amount of matriglycan in muscle from Dag1T190M mice compared to that from C57 mice, the force deficit was not different between the two groups, and centrally nucleated fibers were increased in α-DGN mutant (Dag1T190M) mice by only 1.4-fold.
evidence: This is supported by eccentric contraction data.

claim: Centrally nucleated fibers were increased in Dag1T190M mice by only 1.4-fold compared to C57 mice.
source: However, despite the lower amount of matriglycan in muscle from Dag1T190M mice compared to that from C57 mice, the force deficit was not different between the two groups, and centrally nucleated fibers were increased in α-DGN mutant (Dag1T190M) mice by only 1.4-fold.
evidence: This is supported by histological data.

claim: A matriglycan-positive α-DG over 150 kDa can prevent muscular dystrophy.
source: This indicates that a matriglycan-positive α-DG over 150 kDa can prevent muscular dystrophy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data from different mouse models.

claim: Muscular dystrophy is not observed in a mouse model of Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy, which occurs due to a retrotransposition insertion in the mouse fukutin ortholog and leads to laminin binding at 50% of normal levels.
source: Muscular dystrophy is not observed in a mouse model of Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy, which occurs due to a retrotransposition insertion in the mouse fukutin ortholog and leads to laminin binding at 50% of normal levels (Kanagawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In Dag1T190M mice, the laminin-binding level is about 45% of normal.
source: In Dag1T190M mice, the laminin-binding level is about 45% of normal, which likely explains the mild increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice.
evidence: This is supported by solid-phase binding assay data.

claim: The laminin-binding level of about 45% of normal in Dag1T190M mice likely explains the mild increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice.
source: In Dag1T190M mice, the laminin-binding level is about 45% of normal, which likely explains the mild increase in centrally nucleated fibers compared to muscle from C57 mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding assay and histological data.

claim: In muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice, the laminin-binding level is only 9% relative to that of C57 mice.
source: However, in muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice, the laminin-binding level is only 9% relative to that of C57 mice and leads to a marked increase in centrally nucleated fibers and force deficit induced by lengthening contractions.
evidence: This is supported by solid-phase binding assay data.

claim: The laminin-binding level of only 9% in M-α-DGN KO mice leads to a marked increase in centrally nucleated fibers and force deficit induced by lengthening contractions.
source: However, in muscle from M-α-DGN KO mice, the laminin-binding level is only 9% relative to that of C57 mice and leads to a marked increase in centrally nucleated fibers and force deficit induced by lengthening contractions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding assay, histological, and force measurement data.

claim: Matriglycan length is critical for regulating damage induced by lengthening contractions.
source: This indicates that matriglycan length is critical for regulating damage induced by lengthening contractions and that the production of ~120–150 kDa α-DG significantly prevents dystrophic change, suggesting that this pathologic effect can be prevented without the expression of full-length matriglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data from different mouse models.

claim: The production of ~120–150 kDa α-DG significantly prevents dystrophic change.
source: This indicates that matriglycan length is critical for regulating damage induced by lengthening contractions and that the production of ~120–150 kDa α-DG significantly prevents dystrophic change, suggesting that this pathologic effect can be prevented without the expression of full-length matriglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data from different mouse models.

claim: Dystrophic changes can be prevented without the expression of full-length matriglycan.
source: This indicates that matriglycan length is critical for regulating damage induced by lengthening contractions and that the production of ~120–150 kDa α-DG significantly prevents dystrophic change, suggesting that this pathologic effect can be prevented without the expression of full-length matriglycan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data from different mouse models.

claim: α-DGN is cleaved by the proprotein convertase furin at the sequence RVRR (amino acids 309–312).
source: α-DGN is cleaved by the proprotein convertase furin at the sequence RVRR (amino acids 309–312) (Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: α-DGN has a globular structure that is organized into two subdomains.
source: It has a globular structure that is organized into two subdomains (Brancaccio et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The first subdomain of α-DGN is a typical Ig-like domain.
source: The first subdomain is a typical Ig-like domain; the second subdomain resembles ribosomal RNA-binding proteins (Bozic et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The second subdomain of α-DGN resembles ribosomal RNA-binding proteins.
source: The first subdomain is a typical Ig-like domain; the second subdomain resembles ribosomal RNA-binding proteins (Bozic et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: α-DGN is secreted by cells in culture.
source: α-DGN is secreted by cells in culture (Saito et al., 2011) and has been detected in a wide variety of human bodily fluids, including serum and plasma (Saito et al., 2008; Saito et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: α-DGN has been detected in a wide variety of human bodily fluids, including serum and plasma.
source: α-DGN is secreted by cells in culture (Saito et al., 2011) and has been detected in a wide variety of human bodily fluids, including serum and plasma (Saito et al., 2008; Saito et al., 2011).
